The paper presents an integrated approach to the optimum design of actively controlled composite wings, spanning the disciplines of structures, aerodynamics, and control systems.
The structural modeling uses an equivalent plate analysis approach, which can represent multi-element wing-control surface configurations efficiently.

The unsteady aerodynamics are modeled using the Piecewise Continuous Kernel Function Method (PCKFM), which is reported to be faster and more accurate than the doublet lattice method, especially for configurations with control surfaces.

The paper uses the Minimum State Method for finite-state modeling of the unsteady aerodynamic forces, which can achieve a given level of approximation accuracy with fewer added states compared to other rational function approximation methods.

The goal is to develop a multidisciplinary wing synthesis capability that can effectively model real aircraft wings for preliminary design purposes, bridging the gap between overly simplified and highly detailed analysis models.

The research aims to study the construction of robust approximations to behavior functions to enable efficient multidisciplinary optimization, addressing the heavy computational cost and lack of intuition that are cited as key challenges.

The paper reports that the equivalent plate modeling approach can generate stiffness and mass matrices efficiently using analytic integration, and provides analytic sensitivity derivatives for optimization.

Extensive numerical testing was performed to assess the accuracy of the equivalent plate modeling and unsteady aerodynamics methods, showing good correlation with finite element results and ground vibration test data.
The paper mentions that the first six mode shapes of the YF-16 wing-control surface configuration generated by the equivalent plate analysis correlate well with finite element results.

Typical computation times for static analysis and constraint generation for the YF-16 wing configuration are reported to be 18.9 seconds on an IBM 3090 computer, demonstrating the computational efficiency of the approach.
The paper states that the PCKFM unsteady aerodynamics method is more accurate than the vortex lattice method, especially for configurations with leading edge flaps or control surfaces with gaps.
The Minimum State Method for finite-state modeling of unsteady aerodynamics is reported to reduce the increase in state-space model order compared to other rational function approximation techniques.
The paper highlights the need to cast the aeroservoelastic equations of motion in a linear time-invariant state-space form to enable modern control system analysis and design techniques.

The research is motivated by the recognition that multidisciplinary interactions, including servoaeroelastic effects and rigid body-elastic mode coupling, need to be properly accounted for in the wing design process.
The paper notes that fixes and modifications are still commonly introduced late in the development stage of fighter aircraft when these multidisciplinary effects have not been properly considered.
